In this uncontrolled series of 15 patients with advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck, 10 of 15 (66.7%) achieved clinical tumour reduction. Of the 12 who proceeded to surgery, 5 of 12 (41.7%) had a pathological complete response and 7 of 12 (58.3%) were downstaged. Two patients with apparent clinical lesion resolution chose radiotherapy instead of surgery, and one patient progressed and did not undergo surgery. No grade 3 or higher treatment‑related toxicity was reported.

Clinical disappearance means the lesion is no longer visible or palpable; it does not guarantee microscopic eradication. Pathological complete response confirms absence of viable tumour cells in the resected specimen, a stronger surrogate for cure but still not proof of long‑term disease‑free survival. Durable cure requires sustained absence of recurrence over years, which this study did not assess because follow‑up was short.

Because there was no comparator arm, the series cannot establish that neoadjuvant capecitabine is superior, equivalent, or inferior to standard neoadjuvant regimens or to surgery alone. The absence of high‑grade toxicity in 15 patients suggests tolerability in this small cohort, but rare or delayed adverse events cannot be excluded. Conclusions about comparative efficacy and safety therefore remain speculative.
